subject: chemistry
title: Rate & Equilibrium Adventure 2 · Calculations
welcome_lead: Now we change temperature, pressure and concentration and predict how equilibrium shifts.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry equilibrium shifts — Haber process, contact process, Le Chatelier predictions.
final_note: You can predict equilibrium shifts and explain why industry compromises on conditions.

concepts.def: Heat pushes equilibrium in the endothermic direction
More pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles
Adding a substance shifts equilibrium to use it up
Balance between rate and equilibrium yield

walkthroughs.body_html:
Three things shift equilibrium.

Temperature: raising T pushes equilibrium the endothermic way (it absorbs the extra heat).

Pressure (gases only): raising P pushes towards the side with fewer moles of gas.

Concentration: add a substance and the equilibrium shifts away from it to use it up.

N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ — forward is exothermic. 4 moles of gas on the left, 2 on the right.

For best yield: low temperature (forward is exo) and high pressure (fewer moles on the right).

But low T means a slow rate. So industry uses a compromise: about 450 °C and 200 atmospheres, with an iron catalyst.

2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ — forward is exothermic. 3 moles of gas on the left, 2 on the right.

So lower temperature and higher pressure both favour the product, just like the Haber.

In practice it runs at around 450 °C and only about 2 atmospheres with a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst — the yield is already high so extra pressure isn't worth the cost.

numericals.q: In the Haber reaction N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, how many moles of gas are on the reactant side?
numericals.hint: Count 1 mole N₂ plus 3 moles H₂.

free_texts.q: What word describes the conditions industry chooses to balance yield against rate? One word.
free_texts.hint: Not the best of either — a balance between both.
